pr_body:
Create only one new Fraction object during `limit_denominator()` instead of the four previously made.

Fixes #93476

I believe that each of the calls to `Fraction()` can be called with `_normalize=False` but I have not included that in this PR to limit the scope of changes to the minimum to verify no change in implementation.

Sure, I'll make sure to post some as soon as I have all the tests passing, and run some tests on small denominators, which I didn't do.

`__new__` on Fractions by default runs normalization code which calls math.gcd.  The gcd algorithm runs in O(log n) time, so we'll be eliminating 3 of the 4 calls to that in this code.  It doesn't reduce the algorithmic complexity of this routine, but should be a greater speed up for larger Fraction objects.

We can eliminate the fourth gcd call also if we do not need to retain behavior on an unreduced Fraction created with the private and undocumented keyword `_normalize=False` does not need to maintain backwards compatibility.  (This will speed up calling limit_denominator on Fractions whose denominators is below the limit a lot.)     One example of an existing call that does not guarantee a Fraction that is normalized if the original fraction was not in lowest terms is `__pow__` (and `__rpow__`.   For instance, where `Fraction(3, 12, _normalize=False)**2` returns `Fraction(9, 144)` and not `Fraction(1, 16)`.  Furthermore `3**Fraction(2, 1)` returns `9` (int) while `3**Fraction(4, 2, _normalize=False)` returns `9.0` (float).  Other routines that also give different results with Fractions that skipped normalization are `as_integer_ratio()` (and numerator, denominator, obviously), abs, neg, etc. so I think the general rule for all these methods is to trust that they are being called on a normalized Fraction only.  There was not a discussion about this during the addition of the `_normalize` parameter in Py 3.5: https://bugs.python.org/issue21136

Here are the timing tests I've run.  All fractions checked that they were in lowest terms at declaration.

```

In [9]: %timeit f2.limit_denominator(2_345_679)

# 3.9x limit to small denominator
In [10]: %timeit f1.limit_denominator(1)

In [11]: %timeit f2.limit_denominator(1)

> the general rule for all these methods is to trust that they are being called on a normalized Fraction only

Yes: there shouldn't be any way via the public API to end up with a non-normalised fraction, so methods can reasonably assume that they're operating on normalised fractions. If a `fractions` user is doing things like modifying the `_numerator` or `_denominator` fields of a fraction directly, then they do so at their own risk.

Just to be clear:

> We can eliminate the fourth gcd call also [...]

+1 We should definitely do this.

It's possible that I'm the one who misread it.  If Mark wants to bring this back to life, that would be fine.  My view is that this isn't a method that needs optimizing and think the code should remain as is.  

ISTM that the entire point of the fractions module is to produce a class so that code won't have to handle numerators and denominators separately.  Presumably, any code that uses Fraction could be sped-up by inlining and not using the Fraction class, but that isn't what we've after.   We tend to save inlining for when we really need it.  IMO, the *limit_denominator()* method doesn't qualify.  It is almost never used in a performance critical loop, so it is not a worthy optimization target.

Presumably, any code that uses Fraction could be sped-up by inlining and not using the Fraction class, but that isn't what we've after. We tend to save inlining for when we really need it. IMO, the _limit_denominator()_ method doesn't qualify. It is almost never used in a performance critical loop, so it is not a worthy optimization target.

@rhettinger -- what if the `def _sub(a, b)` call was amended to allow for a private `_normalize: bool` argument.  then it could be:

```
    def _sub(a, b, *, _normalize=True):
        """a - b"""
        na, da = a.numerator, a.denominator
        nb, db = b.numerator, b.denominator
        g = math.gcd(da, db) **if _normalize else 1**
        if g == 1:
            return Fraction(na * db - da * nb, da * db, _normalize=False)
        ....
```

which would allow for using nearly all the original code except that lines like `bound2 - self` would be `bound2._sub(self, _normalize=False)` and be very close to the original w/o inlining?  It would lose the constant-time speedups of this PR, but keep the O(log n) speedups that made the code much faster for most cases.

Libraries that mix float and Fraction (with denominators < a certain number) operations need to call limit_denominator often to know whether a float brought in from non-Python data such as 1/3 is intended to be interpreted as a fraction (my music21 library (600k yearly downloads) and at least two others I've found do this often), so for these cases speed of limit_denominator can be a limiting factor.  Implementing these code speedups alone moved the runtime for the music21 test suite from 8 minutes to 4 minutes.  I'd like give back to the Python community the result of a lot of trial and error for my lab at MIT so others don't need to find the same work arounds.  Thanks!

issue_context.title: Increase speed of Fractions.limit_denominator
issue_context.body:
**Feature or enhancement**

Speed up Fractions.limit_denominator by not creating intermediary Fraction objects

**Pitch**

`Fractions.limit_denominator` returns a new Fraction, but along the way for Fractions > max_denominator creates 3 Fraction objects that are discarded: the fraction farther from the bound and two temporary fractions (`bound1 - self` and `bound2 - shelf`) which are created just for getting their absolute values.

Similar code speedups have been part of the `music21` library since 2015--where we call limit_denominator after every arithmetic operation on note placement--and timing tests give a 7.3x speedup.  (see [music21 Source](https://github.com/cuthbertLab/music21/blob/dcd23748052bfc4e02d5f94a9ff3de5b88ffcb89/music21/common/numberTools.py#L150) )

For fractions with denominators equal to or below max_denominator, instantiate the new Fraction with `Fraction(self._numerator, self._denominator)` instead of `Fraction(self)` for a 23% speedup.

PR to follow.
comments:
In this case, we value algorithmic clarity over a minor performance gain from inlining.  

Also, we would lose some of the recent optimizations in the Fraction class.

The limit_denominator code is almost never in a performance critical section of code, so no one would notice the small benefit, but we would incur a loss of understanding about how it works.

Thanks for the suggestion, but we will decline this one.

review_comments:
I just realised that I'm not 100% convinced that the result here _is_ always normalised. There are two parts to being normalised: the numerator must be relatively prime to the denominator, and the denominator must be positive. I'd thought about the first part (which is fine), but not about the second.

Is it clear that `bound2_d` and `bound1_d` are positive at this point?

Answer: yes, it's true that `bound2_d` and `bound1_d` are positive at this point, though perhaps not 100% clear. In the Euclidean loop above, on the very _first_ iteration `a` can be negative, but on all subsequent iterations `a` is nonnegative. And on the first iteration `q1 = 0`, so that potentially negative `a` does no harm, and `q0` and `q1` are guaranteed nonnegative at all times. Then it's easy to check that they must in fact be positive at the point where the loop exits.
That was my reading of the loop as well, but I didn't write the code (nor name the variables) so I didn't want to change this without another set of eyes; thanks!

We've lost some readability here: the original code clearly expressed the intent "if bound2 is closer to self than bound1 then return bound2, else return bound 1". With this code, I find it much harder to glean that intent.

A comment or two explaining what's going on might help.

I'd also suggest a bit of restructuring to keep things that are closely related together (and to keep consistency with the style of the rest of the function):
```suggestion
        bound1_n, bound1_d = p0 + k*p1, q0 + k*q1
        bound2_n, bound2_d = p1, q1
```
(And yes, there's some small overhead in the tuple packing and unpacking, but I think it's worth keeping for the readability.)
